What is Delftia acidovorans?

Delftia acidovorans is a gram-negative, non-fermentative bacterium first identified in Delft, Netherlands, in soil enriched with acetamide. It thrives in habitats containing high concentrations of heavy metals — copper, cobalt, and even gold — and produces a nonribosomal peptide that allows it to precipitate gold out of solution, avoiding toxicity.

Today, Delftia is found in waste-contaminated soil, water systems, and drains. Beyond its remarkable environmental capabilities, it is studied as an opportunistic pathogen and explored for applications in:

🏅 Gold Biomineralization ♻️ E-Waste Recycling 🌿 Bioremediation 🧬 Genomics 🔬 Undergraduate Research

Research Highlights

Three pillars of the Delftia Project — from the classroom to the community

🎓

Undergraduate Research

Students in MB 360 and LSC 170 engage in hands-on course-based research experiences — growing Delftia in the lab, analyzing spot plates, and dissecting "Microbial Superheroes" publications.

🤖

Genomics & Automation

High-throughput sequencing and automation tools help us decode the genome of Delftia. BLAST analyses, bioinformatics pipelines, and cloud computing accelerate discovery.

🌐

Citizen Science

Community annotators collaborate via Hypothes.is to mine the scientific literature on Delftia as a pathogen, gold-biomineralizing agent, and e-waste recycler.
